entries.citation: Lutz, N. D., Harkotte, M., & Born, J. (2026). Sleep's contribution to memory formation. Physiological Reviews, 106(1), 363-483. (Epub 2025-08-28)

sections_read: PubMed abstract only; publisher page journals.physiology.org returned HTTP 403

entries.design: Narrative review of ~10 years of human and rodent research on sleep-dependent memory consolidation
entries.population: Humans and rodents across the life span (not specific to students)
entries.intervention: Sleep (non-REM slow oscillations, spindles, hippocampal replay; REM)

outcome.measure: Mixed: behavioural retention tests, neural replay/oscillation measures
outcome.transfer: Review discusses memory transformation into more abstract representations; nature of transformation described as controversial

entries.bias_and_applicability: Narrative review, not a systematic quantitative synthesis; mechanistic model (active systems consolidation + synaptic downselection) is the authors' interpretive frame. Abstract explicitly flags open controversies (what is transformed, REM role, sleep vs wake consolidation). Not evidence for any study-scheduling intervention; brain-stimulation enhancement is lab research only.

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C01 consolidation is a mechanism frame, not an instructional rule
R1B-C04 TMR/stimulation are lab-only

entries.citation: Newbury, C. R., Crowley, R., Rastle, K., & Tamminen, J. (2021). Sleep deprivation and memory: Meta-analytic reviews of studies on sleep deprivation before and after learning. Psychological Bulletin, 147(11), 1215-1240.

access.url: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8893218/ (retrieved as PMC XML via NCBI efetch)
sections_read: Method: Search Strategy, Inclusion/Exclusion, Methodological Quality
Results: Meta-Analysis 1 overall, Publication Bias, Moderator Analysis
Results: Meta-Analysis 2 overall, Publication Bias, Moderator Analysis
Discussion: Power-Based Moderators, Publication Bias, Limitations

entries.design: Two meta-analyses of experiments 1970-2020 with at least one full night of total sleep deprivation, before vs after learning
entries.population: Healthy adults; Meta-analysis 1: 45 reports, 130 effect sizes, 1,616 participants, mean age about 22 (Table 1, age reported for 54 effect sizes); Meta-analysis 2: 31 reports, 55 effect sizes, 927 participants
entries.operation: Encoding (pre-learning deprivation) and consolidation (post-learning deprivation) of declarative and procedural material
entries.intervention: Total acute sleep deprivation (>=1 night)

outcome.measure: Objective recognition/recall and motor-skill tasks in lab
outcome.delay: Immediate after deprivation vs after >=1 night recovery sleep (MA1 moderator)

estimate.metric: Hedges' g (memory impairment, deprivation vs sleep)
estimate.value: after learning g = 0.277 (trim-and-fill adjusted 0.166); before learning g = 0.621 (trim-and-fill adjusted 0.463); after learning with recovery sleep before test g = 0.176, without recovery sleep g = 0.410; procedural g = .449 vs declarative g = .218
estimate.ci: after: [0.177, 0.377], adjusted [0.086, 0.247]; before: [0.473, 0.769], adjusted [0.326, 0.601]; recovery-sleep subgroup [0.060, 0.292]; no-recovery subgroup [0.320, 0.499]
estimate.k_or_n: MA1: k = 130 effect sizes / 45 reports / N = 1,616; MA2: k = 55 / 31 reports / N = 927
estimate.note: Mean achieved power of primary experiments to detect the MA1 pooled effect 13.98% (SD 4.60%); MA2 mean power 54.77%; authors caution that trim-and-fill was not designed for multilevel models (Discussion: Publication Bias). Too few recovery-sleep/procedural entries in MA2 for moderator tests.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Full-text checked: literature heavily biased toward young adults and between-group designs (Results MA1 intro, Table 1); very low primary-study power; publication-bias adjustment shrinks but does not eliminate effects. Total one-night deprivation of lab material (word pairs, pictures, motor sequences), not exam-scale learning; recovery-sleep subgroup shows a smaller but non-zero residual deficit, i.e. a later night partly but not fully compensates. Population (healthy young adults) is directly relevant; material and outcome timing are indirect.

claim_edges.locator: Results MA1 'Overall Meta-Analytic Effect Size' and 'Publication Bias' (trim-and-fill)
claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C02 one night of total sleep loss after learning impairs later memory, small effect after bias adjustment

claim_edges.locator: Results MA2 'Overall Sleep Deprivation Effect Size'; Discussion
claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C02b sleep loss before learning impairs encoding (larger pooled effect)
R1B-C02c recovery sleep reduces but does not remove the post-learning deficit

entries.citation: Crowley, R., Alderman, E., Javadi, A.-H., & Tamminen, J. (2024). A systematic and meta-analytic review of the impact of sleep restriction on memory formation. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 167, 105929.
entries.design: Systematic review + meta-analysis of sleep restriction experiments
entries.population: Adults and adolescents in experimental studies (39 reports, 1234 participants)
entries.intervention: Sleep restriction to 3-6.5 h

estimate.metric: Hedges' g (memory impairment, restriction vs normal sleep)
estimate.note: No evidence of publication bias reported; vs 185 total-deprivation effect sizes (Newbury 2021) no significant overall difference; for post-encoding sleep loss, total deprivation associated with larger impairment than restriction

entries.bias_and_applicability: Experimental restriction in labs, often single or few nights; the population mix (adolescents/adults) and material are not exam-scale learning; cross-meta comparison with Newbury is not a randomized contrast. Supports direction for partial sleep loss relevant to exam weeks.

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C02 partial sleep loss (3-6.5 h) impairs memory formation, small effect

entries.citation: Cousins, J. N., Wong, K. F., Raghunath, B. L., Look, C., & Chee, M. W. L. (2019). The long-term memory benefits of a daytime nap compared with cramming. Sleep, 42(1), zsy207.

sections_read: Methods: Participants, Factual knowledge task learning/tests, Table 1

entries.design: Between-group experiment; learning sessions flanking 1 h of nap, break or cramming
entries.population: 84 analysed healthy NUS undergraduates aged 19-27 (wake n = 27, nap n = 27, cram n = 30); biology/ecology majors excluded; no sleep disorders; habitual time in bed ~7.6-7.9 h by actigraphy (Table 1)
entries.intervention: 60-min nap opportunity in lab between learning block pairs (total learning 2 h 20 min across four 40-min self-paced blocks)
entries.comparator: 60 min watching a movie (wake) or 60 min re-studying the same slides (cram)

outcome.measure: 120 two-alternative forced-choice questions per test, separate test sets; 'certain' responses (correct minus incorrect) and hits

estimate.value: nap vs wake: 30 min d = .95, day 8 d = .56; cram vs wake: 30 min d = .60, day 8 d = .27 (n.s.); nap vs cram: 30 min d = .46 (trend, p = .084), day 8 d = .29 (n.s., p = .282)
estimate.note: Group x delay interaction not significant (p = .074). For overall hits only nap vs wake at 30 min was significant.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Single-site, modest n, recognition test of factual material; the abstract's 'napping maintained advantage, cramming did not' is a difference in significance vs wake, not a significant nap-over-cram difference (Results, certain memory). Participants were not sleep-deprived. Supports only: replacing 1 h of extra cramming by a nap did not cost retention in this setting.

claim_edges.locator: Results 'Factual knowledge task' (nap vs cram t-tests)
claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C03 trading rest/sleep for extra cramming time is not a reliable gain at 1 week

entries.citation: Okano, K., Kaczmarzyk, J. R., Dave, N., Gabrieli, J. D. E., & Grossman, J. C. (2019). Sleep quality, duration, and consistency are associated with better academic performance in college students. npj Science of Learning, 4, 16.

sections_read: Results: all subsections incl. Night before assessments, Variance accounted for, Gender differences

entries.design: Prospective correlational study, activity trackers over a semester
entries.population: Introductory college chemistry students (100 enrolled, 88 completed)
entries.intervention: Exposure: tracker-measured sleep duration, quality, consistency

estimate.metric: Pearson r and stepwise regression R^2
estimate.value: sleep duration r = 0.38, sleep quality (Fitbit score) r = 0.44, sleep inconsistency r = -0.36 with overall score; three regressors explained 24.44% of variance, only inconsistency individually significant (p = 0.03); night-before midterm: all rs < 0.20, n.s.
estimate.k_or_n: N = 88 (first 100 volunteers; MIT introductory solid-state chemistry)
estimate.note: Month-before sleep duration correlated with midterm scores rs 0.25-0.34

entries.bias_and_applicability: Observational, volunteers, one elite-institution course, freshmen graded pass/no record; authors note Fitbit 0-10 sleep-quality score lacks published validation and that causality requires RCTs (Discussion). Stepwise regression in N = 88 risks overfitting. Direct population, indirect causal inference.

claim_edges.locator: Results 'Sleep duration, quality, and consistency'; 'Week and month leading up to assessments'
claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C05 sleep regularity over weeks is associated with grades
R1B-C05b no association for the single night before a test (observational null)

entries.citation: Hu, X., Cheng, L. Y., Chiu, M. H., & Paller, K. A. (2020). Promoting memory consolidation during sleep: A meta-analysis of targeted memory reactivation. Psychological Bulletin, 146(3), 218-244.
entries.design: Multilevel meta-analysis of sleep TMR experiments
entries.intervention: Re-presenting learning-associated cues (sounds/odours) during sleep

estimate.value: overall 0.29; NREM2 0.32; SWS 0.27; not effective during REM or wake
estimate.note: Several publication-bias strategies reported in paper (not checked)

entries.bias_and_applicability: Requires sleep-stage-timed cue delivery (polysomnography or closed-loop setup) in controlled settings; no evidence here for unsupervised consumer/app delivery or for exam outcomes. Mechanistic support for reactivation; not a study technique.

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C04 TMR is a lab method; product must not offer 'sleep learning' or cueing features

entries.citation: Shields, G. S., Sazma, M. A., McCullough, A. M., & Yonelinas, A. P. (2017). The effects of acute stress on episodic memory: A meta-analysis and integrative review. Psychological Bulletin, 143(6), 636-675.
entries.design: Random-effects meta-analysis with robust variance estimation; moderator meta-regressions
entries.population: 113 independent human studies, 6,216 participants (mostly young adults, lab stressors such as TSST/cold pressor)
entries.intervention: Acute lab stressor before/during encoding, after encoding, or before retrieval

estimate.value: encoding overall -0.109 (n.s.); post-encoding +0.206; retrieval -0.215 (neutral items -0.136, negative items -0.303)
estimate.k_or_n: encoding m = 33 studies/k = 131 effects/N = 1,607; post-encoding m = 23/k = 83/N = 1,668; retrieval m = 31/k = 102/N = 1,410
estimate.note: Egger asymmetry for encoding and retrieval; trim-and-fill imputed 0 and 1 studies; stressor-encoding delay moderated encoding (impairment after ~22 min); cortisol increase did not moderate effects; post-encoding enhancement eliminated with context change and absent in studies not excluding hormonal-contraceptive users

entries.bias_and_applicability: Lab-induced acute stress with short delays and mostly word/picture lists; exam anxiety and chronic study stress are different exposures. Moderator findings are meta-regressions (associational, small df). Neutral-item retrieval impairment is small.

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C08 acute stress right before retrieval impairs recall on average (small)
R1B-C08b stress is not uniformly harmful: encoding effect phase/timing-dependent, post-encoding often enhancing

entries.citation: Smith, A. M., Floerke, V. A., & Thomas, A. K. (2016). Retrieval practice protects memory against acute stress. Science, 354(6315), 1046-1048.
entries.design: 2 (retrieval practice vs restudy) x 2 (stress vs no stress 24 h later) experiment
entries.intervention: Learning by retrieval practice; acute stress induction before final test
entries.bias_and_applicability: Single study; abstract-level only; 'immune' is a strong word for a non-significant stress effect in the retrieval-practice group (absence of evidence vs equivalence not checked). Simple lab material. Treat as promising interaction, not established protection; see check for replications in report.

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C09 well-practised retrieval may buffer stress-related retrieval impairment (single study)

entries.citation: Ciria, L. F., Román-Caballero, R., Vadillo, M. A., Holgado, D., Luque-Casado, A., Perakakis, P., & Sanabria, D. (2023). An umbrella review of randomized control trials on the effects of physical exercise on cognition. Nature Human Behaviour, 7(6), 928-941. Author Correction: Nat Hum Behav 10(10), 2046 (2026).

sections_read: PubMed record of 2026 Author Correction (no content text available; content of correction not verified)

entries.design: Umbrella review of 24 meta-analyses restricted to RCTs plus meta-analysis of their primary RCTs
entries.population: Healthy population across lifespan (not specific to university students)
entries.intervention: Regular (chronic) physical exercise

estimate.value: 0.22 overall; 0.13 after accounting for active control and baseline differences; 0.05 after publication-bias correction
estimate.k_or_n: 24 meta-analyses; number of primary RCTs not in abstract
estimate.note: An Author Correction was published 2026-10; its content was not accessible in this run and must be checked before citing exact values

entries.bias_and_applicability: Chronic exercise, mostly children/older adults; bias-corrected effect negligible. Does not address acute exercise before/after learning, nor health/well-being benefits of exercise (outside this question).

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C10 'regular exercise boosts cognition/exam performance' is not supported after bias correction in healthy people

entries.citation: Roig, M., Nordbrandt, S., Geertsen, S. S., & Nielsen, J. B. (2013). The effects of cardiovascular exercise on human memory: A review with meta-analysis. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 37(8), 1645-1666.
entries.design: Review with meta-analyses of acute and long-term cardiovascular exercise interventions
entries.population: 29 acute and 21 long-term studies (populations not in abstract)
entries.intervention: Acute bout or long-term cardiovascular exercise

estimate.value: acute on long-term memory 0.52; long-term exercise on long-term memory 0.07 (n.s.); acute on short-term memory 0.26; long-term on short-term memory 0.15
estimate.k_or_n: 'N' in abstract = number of effect comparisons (20, 22, 22, 37) - unit not verified
estimate.note: Molecular priming explanation is mechanistic speculation

entries.bias_and_applicability: 2013, pre-dates bias-sensitive umbrella work; small heterogeneous studies; acute effects on list learning in lab. Indirect to exam study; mechanistic narrative (BDNF priming) not tested here.

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C10b acute exercise around encoding may aid lab memory; small-study evidence, not a study rule

entries.citation: Hagger, M. S., Chatzisarantis, N. L. D., et al. (2016). A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 546-573.
entries.design: Preregistered multi-lab replication of sequential-task paradigm (Sripada et al. protocol)
entries.intervention: Depleting first task (letter-crossing with rule)

estimate.note: CI includes zero

entries.bias_and_applicability: Tests one specific manipulation; does not show that fatigue never exists, only that the brief sequential-task depletion effect is not robust. Supports rejecting 'willpower battery' framing in product copy.

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C06 'willpower is a depletable resource' (strength model) as product rationale

entries.citation: Vohs, K. D., Schmeichel, B. J., Lohmann, S., et al. (2021). A multisite preregistered paradigmatic test of the ego-depletion effect. Psychological Science, 32(10), 1566-1581.

sections_read: PubMed abstract (PMC full-text XML not provided by NCBI/Europe PMC)

entries.design: Preregistered paradigmatic multi-lab replication, two procedures
entries.intervention: One of two depletion procedures

estimate.value: confirmatory d = 0.06 (n.s.); data ~4x more likely under null than informed prior (delta = 0.30, SD 0.15); exploratory full sample d = 0.08
estimate.note: Exploratory: larger effect for participants reporting more fatigue; no moderation by willpower beliefs

entries.bias_and_applicability: Independent of Hagger 2016 lab set and procedure; converging null. Brief lab tasks, not multi-hour study sessions.

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C06 strength-model ego depletion

entries.intervention: n/a

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C07 effort-cost models as competing explanation to depletion

entries.design: Review of computational models (expected value of control) and empirical work

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C07

entries.citation: Albulescu, P., Macsinga, I., Rusu, A., Sulea, C., Bodnaru, A., & Tulbure, B. T. (2022). "Give me a break!" A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance. PLoS ONE, 17(8), e0272460.

sections_read: Risk of bias / Quality of included studies

entries.design: Random-effects meta-analysis of experimental/quasi-experimental studies; Cochrane RoB
entries.population: 22 samples, N = 2,335; 11 student samples and 10 employee samples; 13 lab, 9 workplace
entries.operation: Clerical, cognitive, creative, emotional tasks; not learning/retention
entries.intervention: Micro-break <= 10 min (8 s to 10 min)

outcome.measure: Vigor and fatigue (self-report); performance (objective or self-perceived, mixed)

estimate.value: vigor .36; fatigue .35; overall performance .16 (n.s., p = .116); creative tasks .38; clerical .56; cognitive-task subgroup not significant
estimate.ci: creative [.11, .64]; clerical [0.01, 1.12]; performance publication-bias section reports observed 0.14 [-0.07, 0.36] and trim-and-fill adjusted 0.22 [0.02, 0.43]
estimate.k_or_n: vigor k = 9, n = 913; fatigue k = 9, n = 803; performance k = 15, n = 1,132
estimate.note: Meta-regression: longer breaks associated with larger performance boost. Only 4 of 22 studies low risk of bias. Slight inconsistency between abstract (d = .16) and bias section (d = 0.14) as written.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Outcomes are momentary well-being and task performance, not durable learning; most RoB unclear; break duration not randomized across studies (meta-regression is associational); authors caution against generalizing office work to academic work (Discussion).

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C11 short breaks reduce self-reported fatigue/increase vigor

claim_edges.locator: Results moderator 'type of task'; Discussion para on cognitively demanding tasks

entries.citation: Biwer, F., Wiradhany, W., oude Egbrink, M. G. A., & de Bruin, A. B. H. (2023). Understanding effort regulation: Comparing 'Pomodoro' breaks and self-regulated breaks. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 93(Suppl 2), 353-367.
entries.design: Three-arm online intervention during real self-study for one day (allocation method to be checked)
entries.intervention: Systematic breaks: 6 min after 24-min blocks ('Pomodoro', n = 25) or 3 min after 12-min blocks (n = 27)

outcome.measure: Self-reported fatigue, distractedness, concentration, motivation, mental effort; self-reported task completion

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C12 pre-scheduled breaks are associated with better mood ratings than self-regulated breaks, no learning outcome

claim_edges.locator: abstract RESULTS (no difference in effort or completion)
claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C12b no evidence that a specific Pomodoro interval improves learning

entries.design: Two lab experiments with video lecture segments, interpolated tests vs non-tested conditions

entries.comparator: No interpolated tests / restudy (details not verified)

estimate.note: Current weekly practice estimates exceeded diary-logged practice (F(1,35) = 19.62); by age 20 best and good violinists averaged > 10,000 h practice alone, but this did not separate the groups as in the original

entries.bias_and_applicability: Small expert sample (unavoidable); retrospective estimates are biased upward vs diaries; music performance domain, not exam study. Does not address daily intensity limits.

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C19 core 1993 finding of full correspondence between accumulated practice and skill level

claim_edges.locator: Results 'Comparing weekly practice estimates with diary-recorded practice'

entries.citation: Ericsson, K. A., Krampe, R. T., & Tesch-Römer, C. (1993). The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychological Review, 100(3), 363-406.
entries.source_type: theory + two primary correlational studies (violinists, pianists)

access.url: publicly hosted PDF copy (graphics8.nytimes.com freakonomics blog mirror), read in scratch only, not stored in repo
sections_read: General discussion on maximal sustainable practice pp. 390-392

entries.design: Theoretical framework plus two small cross-sectional studies with retrospective estimates and one diary week
entries.population: Study 1: three groups of 10 Berlin violin students/teachers; Study 2: expert vs amateur pianists
entries.intervention: Exposure: practice alone, sleep, leisure, naps

estimate.value: best two violin groups slept 8.6 h/day vs 7.8 h for music teachers (p. 376); napped 2.8 h/week vs 0.9 h/week (p. 376); expert pianists practised 26.71 h/week solo in diary week (p. 382); 'around 4 hr' daily deliberate practice suggested as a possible general limit (p. 391)
estimate.note: The 4-h figure rests on these small samples, informal interviews (chess, p. 390), anecdotes about writers (pp. 371, 392) and old motor-skill lab studies cited secondarily (p. 370)

entries.bias_and_applicability: Small non-blinded samples (see macnamara2019violin), music domain, self-selected experts; 'effort constraint' is a theoretical postulate; sleep/nap association is cross-sectional and could reflect schedules of conservatory students. The often-cited '4 hours/day' is a hypothesis about elite deliberate practice, not an empirical limit for exam study.

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C20 a universal daily study-hour ceiling is not established; '4 h' is a hypothesis from elite music/chess

claim_edges.locator: p. 376 (sleep 8.6 vs 7.8 h; naps 2.8 vs 0.9 h/week)

entries.citation: Madigan, D. J., & Curran, T. (2021). Does burnout affect academic achievement? A meta-analysis of over 100,000 students. Educational Psychology Review, 33(2), 387-405.
entries.design: Robust-variance meta-analysis of correlations
entries.population: 29 studies, N = 109,396, 89 effect sizes; school, college and university students
entries.intervention: Exposure: student burnout (total, exhaustion, cynicism, reduced efficacy)

outcome.measure: Achievement (objective and subjective; objectivity not a moderator)

estimate.value: total burnout -.24; exhaustion -.15; cynicism -.24; reduced efficacy -.39
estimate.k_or_n: 29 studies, 89 effect sizes, N = 109,396 (total burnout N = 96,169)
estimate.note: I2 about 98% for total burnout; only moderator: instrument for reduced efficacy; publication bias assessed only via fail-safe N

entries.bias_and_applicability: Authors' abstract wording 'burnout leads to worse achievement' overstates a mainly cross-sectional evidence base (their own Limitations); reverse causality acknowledged for efficacy. Fail-safe N is a weak bias test. Relevant population includes university students.

claim_edges.r1b_claim: R1B-C24 burnout symptoms co-occur with lower achievement (association, causal direction open)

entries.citation: Wendsche, J., & Lohmann-Haislah, A. (2017). A meta-analysis on antecedents and outcomes of detachment from work. Frontiers in Psychology, 7, 2072.

estimate.note: heavy work investment negatively related to detachment (medium)
